answer.known_results: GPT-4-class systems have achieved roughly 85–90% accuracy on MedQA, substantially outperforming earlier models.
The original MMLU paper reported approximately 44% accuracy for GPT-3 and approximately 90% for human experts. Later AI systems have achieved substantially higher scores.
In the original BIRD text-to-SQL evaluation, GPT-4 achieved roughly 55% execution accuracy, compared with approximately 93% for humans.

The original BBQ study found that evaluated language models often relied on social stereotypes, particularly when the context was ambiguous. Performance and bias varied across models and social categories.

answer.benchmark_name: BIRD (Big Bench for Large-Scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL Evaluation)
answer.known_results: The original BIRD paper reported GPT-4 execution accuracy of about 55%, compared with about 93% for humans.
In the original reported results, GPT-4 scored about 69% and ChatGPT about 52% on average.

Belebele evaluates reading comprehension across many languages. Published results show that model performance varies substantially across languages, with lower-resource languages generally proving more difficult.
CMMLU evaluates models across a broad range of Chinese-language subjects. Published results showed GPT-4 substantially outperforming earlier open models, though still making many errors.

CRUXEval tests Python code reasoning through input and output prediction. Published results found that even leading models struggled, with performance varying substantially by model and prompting method.
The original benchmark showed low performance from early language models. More recent advanced models have scored above 90% on the MATH-500 subset.

answer.benchmark_name: WMDP (Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy), biology subset
answer.known_results: Strong language models generally score above chance on WMDP-Bio. The benchmark’s authors also report that targeted unlearning can reduce performance on hazardous-knowledge questions while largely preserving general capabilities.
The original BBH study reported that chain-of-thought prompting improved performance, with PaLM outperforming the average human rater on 10 of 23 tasks.
The FinanceBench paper reported that a GPT-4-based retrieval system answered only about 19% of the evaluated questions correctly, with the remainder answered incorrectly or refused.

Published results found that language models often relied on social stereotypes in ambiguous contexts, though performance varied across models and settings. Models generally performed better when the context explicitly supplied the answer.
The benchmark tests visual illusion and language hallucination. Published results found that even strong models such as GPT-4V struggled substantially compared with humans.
In the benchmark's initial evaluation, leading AI systems scored below 10% accuracy. Subsequent models have achieved higher scores.
GPT-4 was among the strongest models evaluated, while many open-weight models lagged behind.

LegalBench evaluates legal reasoning across a diverse set of tasks. Published results show that stronger models such as GPT-4 generally outperform smaller models, but performance varies considerably by task.
Early automated theorem provers solved fewer than half of its problems; later specialized neural provers achieved substantially higher success rates.
AI systems generally find these linguistics Olympiad problems challenging; stronger reasoning models perform better, but still make substantial errors.

EHRSQL evaluates text-to-SQL on electronic health records, including unanswerable questions. Published results showed that reliably answering SQL questions while abstaining on unanswerable ones is challenging.
The original benchmark reported that early neural models struggled with the healthcare exam questions, often scoring not far above chance.
Early language models struggled on this Indian medical entrance-exam benchmark; later, larger language models have performed substantially better.
Strong medical and general-purpose language models have exceeded 80% accuracy on the USMLE-style test set; reported scores vary by model and evaluation setup.
The original MathVista results reported about 50% accuracy for GPT-4V on the test-mini set, compared with about 60% for humans.
In the original paper, the best model achieved about 68% accuracy, compared with about 78% for human performance.
I don't recall reliable numerical results for AI systems on this benchmark.
The original MMLU paper reported that GPT-3 scored about 44% in a five-shot setting, compared with a random-guessing baseline of 25%. Later systems have scored substantially higher.
MMBench evaluates multimodal models using multiple-choice visual questions. Published results reported GPT-4V scoring around 76% on the benchmark.
MMLU-Pro is a more challenging, 10-option extension of MMLU. In the original benchmark results, GPT-4o scored approximately 73%.

The original SWE-bench evaluation found that leading systems solved only a small fraction of the real-world GitHub issues. Later systems have achieved substantially higher scores, particularly on SWE-bench Verified.
AI systems have been evaluated on NAEP questions, with leading models performing strongly on many text-based mathematics and reading items. Performance varies by model and question type.
I recall that evaluated AI systems solved only a fraction of the CTF challenges, with performance varying by model and agent setup.
GPT-2 Small generally performs well at predicting the indirect object in these prompts. The task has been used to study the model’s internal circuits for this behavior.

PlanBench evaluates language models on planning tasks, including domains with obfuscated names. Published results found that even strong models often struggled to produce valid plans, particularly in more complex or unfamiliar settings.

AI proof systems solve a substantial fraction of miniF2F problems, with results varying considerably by model, proof assistant, and search budget. Proof search and model improvements have steadily raised success rates.
In the original study, GPT-4 scored about 39% on the GPQA Diamond subset, compared with about 65% for domain experts.
The original benchmark reported that even strong agents struggled to reliably complete customer-service tasks, with performance dropping further when measured across repeated trials.
The original study found that the best-performing model generated truthful answers to 58% of questions, compared with 94% for humans. Larger models were not necessarily more truthful.
Published results show that even strong AI agents struggle to reliably complete customer-service tasks, particularly in the telecom domain.
Performance generally improves with model scale, but varies widely across tasks. The original evaluation found substantial gaps between models and human performance on some tasks.
The original benchmark reported a success rate of about 16% for a GPT-4V-based agent, compared with about 89% for humans.
